title: Start AI automation with one boring workflow
metaTitle: AI automation for small business, one chore
excerpt: Start AI automation with one repeated chore that has a clear input and a clear output. Skip the platform that promises to automate the whole company.
alt: Two people pointing at a laptop screen, one wearing a fitness band. The shared screen is a single workflow being checked, which is the right size for a first automation.
caption: One screen, one chore, one check. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What is a good first automation for a small business?
faqs.answer: Pick a repeated chore with a trigger, an input, an output, and a person who can check the result quickly. Status replies, file delivery, and intake forms are common shapes. Leave taste and the judgment a customer is paying for with a person.

faqs.question: How many workflows should we start with?
faqs.answer: Start with one path, watch the first runs, and stop there until it is dull and correct. Stacking several chores on day one means you cannot tell which step failed. A second workflow is allowed once the first has had a quiet week and still has its own review.

faqs.question: What if review takes longer than the old chore?
faqs.answer: Remove the automation. Compare the minutes of the old chore with the minutes of review over a normal week, timed on real runs rather than a demo. A longer review means the workflow was not shaped enough to hand to a machine. Doing the chore by hand is a successful result.

markdown:
AI automation for small business should start as one boring workflow with a clear input and a clear output. A person can point at the chore, say what goes in, say what should come out, and check the result in a minute. A platform that promises to automate the company has no such edge. It asks you to reorganize the work before you have learned whether a single step was worth removing.

Boring is the filter. If the chore is repeated, dull, and already written down somewhere, it is a candidate. If it requires taste, a relationship, or a judgment call the customer is paying for, leave it with a person.

## Pick the chore by its shape

Look at last week and list the tasks someone did more than five times. Ignore the ones that felt important. The important ones are usually the judgment. Keep the ones that felt like copying.

A useful candidate has four properties.

- A trigger you can name. A form is submitted, an invoice is paid, a message arrives with a known subject.
- An input with a shape. A name, an email, a file, a status. Not "the customer's vibe."
- An output with a shape. A row in a sheet, a message in a known channel, a draft sitting in a folder for review.
- A person who can tell, quickly, whether the output is right.

An example, labeled as an exercise and not as a client project: a studio receives the same "please send the logo files" request several times a week. The input is the request. The output is the current logo pack and a short note about which file to use. That chore is boring, repeated, and checkable. Automating the design critique that decides the logo is a different project, and a worse one.

If you cannot describe the output before you pick a tool, you are shopping for software, not removing a chore.

A second filter helps when several chores look equally dull. Prefer the one a customer already waits on. A late logo pack, a status that someone has to ask for, or a handoff that stalls a colleague is worth more than a tidy internal report nobody reads. Prefer a chore whose mistakes are visible. If a wrong output would sit unnoticed for a month, you cannot review it, and you should not automate it yet.

## One workflow, then stop

Build the single path. When the trigger fires, the workflow gathers the input, produces the output, and stops. It does not also update the CRM, post to social, and rewrite the homepage. Those can be later workflows, each with its own check. Stacking them on day one means you cannot tell which step failed.

Choose the smallest tool that can see the trigger and write the output. A mail rule, a short script, a bot with three commands, or a model that drafts a reply from a template. The tool is not the point. The point is that the old chore no longer requires someone to remember it.

Hanabi builds small automations, including Telegram and Discord bots, when a workflow is specific enough to deserve one. Specific means the command list is short and the result is something a person already knew how to produce by hand. A bot that "runs the business" is a slogan. A bot that answers "where is my file" from a known folder is a workflow.

Keep a person on the first twenty runs. Watch the failures. Adjust the input rules. Only then let it run with a lighter check. The first week is part of the build. Skipping it is how a confident wrong message reaches a customer.

## What you leave alone

Leave the work that is the product. For a studio, that is the design judgment and the writing of the offer. For a shop, that is the decision about what the product is and how it should be described when the facts are not already in the catalog. For a software company, that is the choice of what the interface should help someone do.

Also leave anything you cannot undo without embarrassment. Sending a payment, deleting a record, or emailing a customer a price should wait on a person until the workflow has been dull and correct for a while. Drafting is a fine output. Sending is a separate, later decision.

The W3C notes that the [Web Content Accessibility Guidelines](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) apply to AI web interfaces, and that the guidelines sit under four principles, including understandable and operable. If the workflow's output is something a person must read or act on, write it so the action and the result are plain. A clever summary that hides what happened is not a finished automation. It is a new chore called "decode the summary."

## How you will know it worked

Before you turn it on, write down the minutes. How long did the chore take last week, including the hunting for the file and the retyping? How long will a review of the output take? If you do not know, time five real runs of the old way. A guess will flatter the tool.

The comparison that matters is old minutes against review minutes, over a normal week. If review takes longer than the chore, remove the automation and do the chore by hand. That is a successful experiment. You learned the workflow was not boring enough, or not shaped enough, to hand to a machine.

Do not add a second workflow to "make the platform worth it." The platform does not need to be worth it. The chore does. A second workflow is allowed when the first one has been quiet and correct, and when it has its own input, output, and review.

The piece that goes further on that comparison is [how to tell whether an automation saved time](/blog/did-the-automation-save-time). Read it when the first workflow has been running long enough to time honestly.
